While the story is told from a single first-person point of view, the narrator successfully captures the distinct, believable perspectives of a wide range of characters reacting to the same prolonged crisis. We see the viewpoint of Priya, a vulnerable, pregnant junior faculty member who initially feels pressured to find the dysfunction "charming" to protect her tenure prospects; Margaret, the beleaguered department chair trapped in the "helpless decency of a middle manager"; and Ray and Gerry, the working-class maintenance and construction men who view the building's physical stubbornness with a mix of genuine grief, poetic resignation, and earnest optimism. 

Furthermore, the story features a notably difficult and prickly character in Professor Lindqvist, who regards "all change as a personal affront," fights a "war against metaphor," and engages in passive-aggressive bureaucratic spats with the chair. Despite his curmudgeonly nature, the narrative portrays his perspective convincingly and with great empathy—showing him quietly emptying water buckets at eight in the morning and ultimately delivering a resonant, philosophical reflection at his retirement about the universal nature of institutional decay. Even the distant, bureaucratic perspective of the university administration (the Provost's office and the air-quality assessors) is rendered with a wry, recognizable accuracy through their evasive, liability-minded language.
